body.text: It was an outcome none anticipated. Local body elections normally favour the incumbent party in power. Yet, in the recently held elections to the urban local bodies in Rajasthan on September 9 and 11, the BJP under the stewardship of Bhajan Lal Sharma barely scraped through with a 0.94 per cent vote share margin, with a resurgent Congress in tow. What was even more surprising was the election of a large number of independents, including from Bharatpur, the home district of the Chief Minister. Most of the independents who got elected across the State were rebels who were denied tickets, mostly from the Congress and the BJP.

The Congress could have swung these elections in its favour, given the less than 1 per cent vote share margin. This translated to around 99,000 votes, a figure which, sources said, could have easily been garnered across the State. Sources said that the Pradesh Congress Committee (PCC) had a lot to answer for. Even though the Congress under PCC chief Govind Singh Dotasra did mount a campaign centred around governance issues against the BJP, there were issues in the process of candidate selection, which was less consultative and more centralised.

As for the not-so-decisive win by the BJP, it was nevertheless hailed by all its leaders, including Prime Minister Modi, who claimed the party’s victory was that of “truth” over “falsehood”. It was a vindication, he said, of double-engine governance both at the State and the Centre. What party apparatchiks glossed over conveniently was the defeat of the party in strongholds like Jhalawar, a bastion of former Chief Minister Vasundhara Raje, and Bharatpur, the karmabhoomi of Chief Minister Bhajan Lal Sharma. Bharatpur adjoins Uttar Pradesh, and political observers say that the election outcome in Rajasthan, with a large number of independents getting elected in the Bharatpur municipal corporation, could resonate in the Uttar Pradesh elections next year. The BJP forfeited Ajmer, Jhalawar, and Bharatpur, all considered party strongholds.
A fragile victory

A break-up of the votes tells a story of how fragile the BJP’s victory has been and what it may bode for the State Assembly election, two years from now, in 2028. Across the 309 urban local bodies, the BJP secured 35.18 per cent, Congress 34.24 per cent, Independents 27.38 per cent; NOTA constituted 1.03 per cent, which was more than the vote share of many established parties—the Rashtriya Loktantrik Party (0.94 per cent), the Aam Aadmi Party (0.46 per cent), the Communist Party of India (Marxist) (0.32 per cent), the Bahujan Samaj Party (0.28 per cent), and the Bharat Adivasi Party (0.13 per cent). In terms of the number of wards won, of the 10,245 wards, the BJP won 4,182, Congress 3,619, Independents 2,273, RLP 63, AAP 42, CPI(M) 38, BSP 19, and the BAP 8. The election was not held in Ward No. 2 of the Tonk Municipal Council.

Amra Ram, CPI(M) Lok Sabha MP from Sikar, told Frontline that the vote-share trends were important pointers. While elections in the State, right from panchayat levels to Parliament, had always displayed a bipolar character, with vote shares almost equally divided between the two major parties, the emergence of a large number of independents showed that people were looking for alternatives other than the BJP and Congress. He said the delay in holding elections had gone against the ruling party. The government, instead of holding elections to local bodies, had appointed administrators to run both urban and rural local bodies, as it somewhere realised that the public mood was against it.

It was only after the court intervened that the elections were held, Amra Ram said, and in many corporations the BJP fell short of a majority. Because the Congress was seen as the immediate alternative, it became the chief beneficiary of the anti-BJP mood in some cases, but the large number of independents elected showed that people were looking past both major parties. He attributed this to the shared impact of economic policy on ordinary voters, who did not distinguish between the two, and pointed to farmers’, students’ and industrial unrest, including in Rajasthan, as contributing factors.

He predicted similar results in the panchayat elections, adding pointedly: “They made big slogans like ek pradesh, ek chunaav [one State, one election]. But they are unable to even hold local body elections at the same time.” The rising cost of living had also hurt the BJP, he said—public medical education, in particular, had grown far more expensive. “Fifteen years ago, the fees for a medical college were a few thousand rupees. Today, it is in lakhs. A NREGA worker could afford to educate her children at a government medical college at present wages, but no longer,” he said.

The BJP had broken all norms too, he said. In Mandawa town (Jhunjhunu district), the police entered a hotel and picked up opposition party members on the pretext of conducting a search. As mayoral and chairperson elections were yet to happen, he said there were reports of intimidation and coercion to get elected persons to switch over to the BJP. Cases were registered against non-BJP candidates and councillors before the elections. To prevent poaching, both parties had housed their elected candidates in hotels.

Both Gen Z and millennials comprised 43.7 per cent of the population, Amra Ram said, and the crackdown on the youth in Delhi in July had an impact on the local polls. “There’s tremendous frustration among them. In every government department, there are two kinds of employees, one on contract and the other permanent. In almost all the State universities, there are a large number of vacancies. No one gets a patta [land plot] without bribing their way through in the local bodies,” he said.
Gehlot and the delay in polls

Ashok Gehlot, veteran Congress leader and former three-time Chief Minister, also spoke on similar lines when he addressed the media in Jaipur. He said the BJP could not get a decisive edge over its rivals despite the misuse of state machinery, money power, and the delimitation of wards and bodies. He also pointed out how the BJP had lost in the home turfs of almost all of its State leadership. He alleged discriminatory police action against the Opposition, intimidation, and the offering of inducements to councillors to support BJP candidates for mayoral posts.

Interestingly, the polls to the municipalities were supposed to be held in January this year, following the expiry of the term of the local bodies. The panchayat elections too had been delayed by over a year. It was only after the Rajasthan High Court intervened that the dates for the urban polls were announced, but even then the government sought postponement on some ground or the other. Despite the court ordering that elections be held in April 2026, the government sought deferment of the dates on the ground that a report by the OBC Commission (on reservations) was awaited. Contempt notices were issued to the State Election Commission and the Election Commissioner.

The Congress and other opposition parties criticised the government for delaying the polls, with the former carrying out a State-wide campaign demanding timely polls. Then, in July 2026, a Division Bench of the High Court ruled that the government had to hold elections to both panchayats and local bodies by November 2026, and no more delays would be accepted. The State Election Commission provided a schedule for both elections. While elections to the local bodies were held in early September, the panchayat elections are expected to be completed by November.

Talking to Frontline, Raghavendra Mirdha, a PCC secretary, said there was no real explanation for the delay in holding the local body elections. They should have been held after the expiry of the term of the urban and rural local bodies, he said. Compared with other parties, the BJP had left no stone unturned to win these elections, as much of its State leadership was deeply involved in the campaigning. “This kind of involvement by the State leadership was unprecedented. Still, despite the Chief Minister treating these elections as an Assembly election, with road shows in nine places, the BJP’s victory wasn’t a convincing one,” he said.

As for his own party, he felt the Congress could have fared much better, given the anti-incumbency against the government. Congress leaders like Mirdha were rather shocked that votes polled under NOTA were more than the winning margin between the BJP and the Congress. “Are we so bad that people preferred NOTA rather than the Congress? There has to be serious introspection,” he said.

There have been various off-the-cuff explanations for the Congress’s performance. According to sources, the party’s bottom-up strategy through its Sangathan Srujan Abhiyaan for organisational rejuvenation and restructuring had not taken off in the manner intended. It was mostly on paper. This nationwide campaign was launched in April last year by the central leadership with the idea of rejuvenating the organisation. All India Congress Committee observers were appointed for selecting district Congress presidents.

But sources said that while there were booth-level workers, there was no chain of command. There was a feeling that the centralised control by the AICC and PCC needed a rethink. There was no human connect, said sources. There was a delimitation and decentralisation of the organisational set-up but no decentralisation in the selection of candidates. “Had the District Congress Committee heads taken everyone into confidence, including village-level functionaries, we could have easily swung these elections in our favour. It doesn’t work when a local-level AICC functionary gives an order to booth-level workers, ignoring the middle order. Had there been a cohesive campaign, we would have done much better, as anti-incumbency against the incumbent government is very strong,” said sources.

There were instances of sitting chairpersons not being consulted. In Nagaur, for example, one left the party and joined the BJP; the other stayed at home and didn’t campaign. “In an election, or an Indian family wedding, all the phuphajis [uncles] have to be involved,” quipped a source, referring to the phrase naraaz phuphaa (angry uncles) coined by Narendra Modi to describe the Congress and the opposition.
What it means for 2028

Commenting on the poll outcome, Rajiv Gupta, retired professor of sociology at Rajasthan University, said the BJP had lost the character of a ruling party, given how narrowly it had won. The party appeared to be losing popularity in urban areas, he told Frontline, and this time people had not voted on caste or religious lines, which was itself a reason so many independents got elected—the AAP won a majority in Baran, the CPI(M) in Nokha, and independents prevailed in Bikaner and elsewhere.

What troubled him more was the “subversion of democracy” in the process that followed the vote: even a party with a majority could not be sure which of its own would hold the top offices in an urban body, since “councillors have become a saleable commodity.” He pointed to the use of money and muscle power to buy councillors from both the Congress and the independents, and to the practice of housing councillors in hotels to prevent poaching. “It is tragic that even the Congress is unable to hold on to its own victorious candidates,” he observed.

The Assembly elections for 200 seats in Rajasthan are due in December 2028, two years from now. In the 2023 Assembly election, the BJP won 115 seats, 15 more than the cut-off required for a simple majority. Vasundhara Raje was sidelined, and, to the annoyance of many State satraps, a relatively obscure face was chosen to lead the State. Raje was later accommodated at the Centre as one of the 13 national vice-presidents. Sources said that she didn’t campaign much in the urban polls, which could have been a reason for the Congress wresting the majority of seats in Jhalawar, which adjoins Madhya Pradesh.

Traditionally, the BJP has always been viewed as an “urban” party, though in recent years it has made inroads among rural voters, displacing parties like the Congress and others. But its wafer-thin victory in the recent urban polls, and that too within three years of forming the government, could be a pointer of things to come in 2028.
